clue.text: Chubby harpist, Edenic resident — unearthly being, primarily!

definitions.text: Chubby harpist, Edenic resident — unearthly being, primarily!

indicators.note: take each word's primary, i.e. first, letter

explanation.surface: A portrait of a plump little angel strumming a harp in paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: read straight it describes a cherub, and its six first letters spell one.
explanation.definitionFit: A cherub is the chubby winged angel of paintings, often shown with a harp in heaven.

clue.text: Fruit, N. European, for Tom Sawyer's pal

parts.note: a huckleberry is a small dark berry
a Finn comes from Finland, in northern Europe

explanation.surface: A list of foods and nationalities that turns into a question about Mark Twain.
explanation.walkthrough: The two parts sit in the clue in the same order as in the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Huckleberry Finn is Tom Sawyer's friend in Mark Twain's novels.

clue.text: Ken Starr not quite liberal, extremely gross

indicators.note: not the whole word: STARR loses its final letter
free and loose with the letters, so rearrange them

explanation.surface: A political jibe at Ken Starr, the US prosecutor who investigated Bill Clinton, as far from liberal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal' reads as a political label for Starr; it is the instruction to rearrange KEN STAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Rankest is the superlative of rank, meaning gross or foul, so 'extremely gross'.

clue.text: Bastille's stormed, tougher than the rest

indicators.note: a stormed fortress is broken open and its contents thrown about

explanation.surface: A cry from the French Revolution, when the Bastille prison was stormed by the toughest of the mob.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in Bastille's is ignored, leaving nine letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballsy means gutsy or tough; the ballsiest is the toughest of all.

clue.text: Tiny something taken by secretary

definitions.meaning: an adjective for very small, said my-NEWT
a secretary takes notes of a meeting; one such note, said MIN-it

explanation.surface: An office scene where the secretary is handed some small item.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are pronounced differently, which hides the link: my-NEWT for tiny, MIN-it for the note.
explanation.definitionFit: Minute means tiny, and a secretary takes the minutes of a meeting.

clue.text: Biblical lawgiver saunters with yen to depart

indicators.note: to depart is to leave, so the yen leaves the word it sits in

parts.note: to mosey is to stroll along
Y is the abbreviation for yen, the Japanese currency; it is removed from MOSEYS

explanation.surface: An Old Testament prophet ambling away with a longing to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yen' looks like a craving to be off; it is the currency's abbreviation Y, taken out of MOSEYS.
explanation.definitionFit: Moses received the Ten Commandments and gave the Law to the Israelites.

clue.text: Book with the writer supporting N. African capital — not about Kenyan city

indicators.note: in a down answer, what supports sits underneath

parts.note: the writer refers to the setter: I

explanation.surface: A travel writer propping up a book about North African capitals.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is built bottom-up: B and I 'support' N and AIRO from below in the down light.
explanation.definitionFit: A city named by its country: Kenya's capital and largest city.

clue.text: Inane, thick tot — he misbehaves — grin and bear it

indicators.note: the letters behave badly and move out of order

explanation.surface: A harassed parent enduring a silly toddler's bad behaviour through gritted teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: The unkind description of the child is simply the letter supply; the parent's patience is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To take it on the chin is to accept a blow or setback without complaint.

clue.text: Jack's obstacle making Cedric and Les tickled in part

indicators.note: the answer is only part of the run of words

explanation.surface: Two men named Cedric and Les being tickled by a sailor's hurdle.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the nursery rhyme 'Jack be nimble, Jack be quick, Jack jump over the candlestick'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nursery rhyme, Jack has to jump over the candlestick.

clue.text: Drug-addled greeting heard

indicators.note: what is heard is the sound, not the spelling

parts.note: hi is a greeting; say it aloud

explanation.surface: Someone stoned mumbling a hello.
explanation.walkthrough: HI and HIGH are spoken identically.
explanation.definitionFit: To be high is to be under the influence of drugs.

clue.text: Tax riverside protection in announcement

indicators.note: an announcement is spoken, so the word is taken by sound

parts.note: a levee is an embankment against flooding

explanation.surface: A government announcing a charge to pay for flood defences.
explanation.walkthrough: A levee is a raised bank built along a river to stop it flooding; LEVEE and LEVY are said the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: A levy is a tax or charge imposed by an authority.

clue.text: Everyman's going to heads, having complaints

parts.note: the setter says 'I'll', short for I will
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness's neighbour Dungeness

explanation.surface: The setter off to see the bosses with a list of grievances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heads' looks like bosses or the toilet; it means headlands, NESSES, a word seen in place names like Dungeness.
explanation.definitionFit: Complaint is the doctor's word for an ailment, the sense hidden behind the grumbling one the surface suggests.

clue.text: Express view in ode to a Christmas tree?

parts.note: the poetic 'O' that opens an address in an ode
a pine is a typical Christmas tree

explanation.surface: A poet offering an opinion by way of a hymn to the festive tree, like the carol O Tannenbaum.
explanation.walkthrough: The ode would begin 'O pine!', the way an ode addresses its subject; run together it gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, slightly formal: to put your opinion into words.

clue.text: Slapdash, a bit, UEFA's only partly regular

indicators.note: the answer is a part of the words that precede it

explanation.surface: A complaint that UEFA, European football's governing body, is careless and inconsistent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regular' looks like part of the complaint about UEFA; it is the definition, a regular customer.
explanation.definitionFit: A habitué is a frequent visitor to a place, a regular.

clue.text: Leaves by swish old railway

explanation.surface: Someone departing on a smart vintage train line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' reads as a verb, departs; it is a noun, salad leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicory is a plant grown for its bitter salad leaves.

clue.text: Stop using smartphones, laptops etc? As if

definitions.meaning: come off = give up; IT = information technology
both are scornful expressions of disbelief

explanation.surface: Advice to take a break from screens, met with a scoffing reply.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful reading: IT is information technology, and you come off it as you would a drug.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Come off it!' and 'As if!' both mean 'I don't believe you'.

clue.text: Kind of tense? Ideal

definitions.meaning: grammar names tenses: past, present, future, and the one for completed action, as in 'I have eaten'
an adjective: flawless, the best possible

explanation.walkthrough: The perfect is a grammatical tense for completed action; the second sense is the everyday one.
explanation.definitionFit: Perfect names a tense in grammar and also means ideal.

clue.text: What the crossword setter sees as exquisite, friends!

indicators.text: What the crossword setter sees as

parts.note: slap-up = excellent, as in a slap-up meal; the UP is read as an instruction

explanation.surface: The setter gushing to solvers about something lovely.
explanation.walkthrough: Slap-up is British for lavish or first-rate. A setter reads 'SLAP up' literally: in a down entry, SLAP written upwards reads PALS.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: pal is informal English for a friend, suiting the setter's chummy 'friends!'.

clue.text: Tangled dungarees abandoned by Dutch causes vexation

indicators.note: what is abandoned is left behind, so the Dutch abbreviation walks away from the word

parts.note: Du. = Dutch; removed from DUNGAREES to leave NGAREES

explanation.surface: Someone infuriated by snarled-up work trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: Du. is the dictionary abbreviation for Dutch. Remove it from the front of DUNGAREES, then rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrage is to make furious, to cause vexation.

clue.text: Twerp in middle of heath finding track

parts.note: a moor is open heathland; split MO|OR

explanation.surface: A fool out on the heath who stumbles on a path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Track' looks like a noun, a path on the heath; it is a verb, to follow closely.
explanation.definitionFit: To monitor something is to track it, keeping watch over it.

clue.text: Taking home fishing kit

definitions.meaning: take-home pay is what you earn after tax, i.e. your net pay

explanation.surface: An angler bringing their gear back after a trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking home' means pay after deductions, take-home pay, not carrying things home.
explanation.definitionFit: Netting is both clearing a sum as profit and the mesh fishermen use.

clue.text: Schedule a hill to climb

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means reading upwards

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A walking itinerary with a hill to climb.
explanation.walkthrough: A tor is a rocky hilltop in the West of England.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, mainly British: a list setting out who takes which turn or duty.

clue.text: Coat chicken?

definitions.meaning: a coat of paint is one thickness spread over a surface
a hen kept for laying eggs; the question mark marks it as one example

explanation.surface: Instructions to coat a chicken, as in a recipe.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a cooking instruction; both words are nouns, a coat of paint and a laying hen.
explanation.definitionFit: A layer is a coating and also a hen that lays eggs.

clue.text: King, extremely stuck up, beheaded: most awkward!

indicators.note: a word's head is its first letter, so cutting it off removes the S

parts.note: SNOTTIEST without its first letter S

explanation.surface: A haughty king, loathed for his arrogance, is executed.
explanation.walkthrough: Snotty means snobbish, so 'extremely stuck up' is SNOTTIEST before its head comes off.
explanation.definitionFit: A knotty problem is a tricky one; the knottiest is the most awkward.

clue.text: Merry after skipping starter: broken bread in Scandinavia

indicators.note: tipsy and unsteady, so the letters reel about

parts.note: BROKEN without its first letter B

explanation.surface: A cheerful diner who skipped the first course breaking bread on a Nordic trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread' is slang for money, so the definition is a currency. 'Merry' starts the clue looking like a mood; it tells you to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The krone is the currency of Denmark and Norway, and bread is slang for money.

clue.text: Oath: if doing, perform honestly

indicators.note: the letters perform, putting on a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A sworn promise to act with integrity if called upon.
explanation.walkthrough: The oath theme fits the answer nicely, but 'Oath' is fodder, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To act in good faith is to act honestly, without intent to deceive.

clue.text: For himself, the king's — that is to say — casual apparel

parts.note: a king speaking of his own things says 'one's'

explanation.surface: A monarch, speaking of his own wardrobe, describes his loungewear.
explanation.walkthrough: Royals traditionally say 'one' for 'I', so the king's word for 'my' is ONE'S.
explanation.definitionFit: A onesie is a loose all-in-one garment worn for lounging.

clue.text: Cheers! Drink, then eastern casserole

parts.note: ta = thanks, as is cheers in British speech
surface padding: the next piece follows on

explanation.surface: A toast, a drink, and then a spicy stew from the East for dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'Cheers!' and 'Ta!' both mean thanks, not only a toast.
explanation.definitionFit: A tagine is a slow-cooked North African stew, named after its pot.
